entry.title: On the Mechanistic Function of the Recurrent Block in Looped Transformers, Part 1

link.title: On the Mechanistic Function of the Recurrent Block in Looped Transformers, Part 1

entry.content:
tl;dr: I take toy-scale versions of two plain looped transformers that differ in where their norms sit, a Huginn-style looped transformer, and a one-layer transformer baseline, train them on 1, 2, and 3-hop modular addition chains mod 113 using the recipe from Nanda et al. (2023), and measure generalization on up to 6-hop chains. I switch to gradient clipping and learning rate decay late in training to address training instability under the recipe’s constant learning rate and high weight decay with AdamW, and observe the mechanistic function of the recurrent components of the resulting looped models. I find that none of the loops work through the chain one operation at a time, instead using even attention from the = token to gather inputs, as the one-layer model does, and reading the answer off a clock of the total in all but one trial (which did use a clock at another seed, so this depends on the seed). The loops with a clock also hold up better at 6 hops than the one-layer model (0.88–0.93 accuracy, against 0.60–0.79), though the one-layer model didn’t get the clipping and decay. I also find that in the plain loops, a linear probe reads the answer from the loop’s state several passes before the model’s own output does. More hops delay this probe by anywhere from 2-4 passes, but the output by at most 1. Accuracy at the training depth hides the differences in how the looped models use their recurrent block. The plain loops break when run past their training depth, and the Huginn-style loop even ends training ignoring its carried state, relying only on the re-injected input.

This work is accompanied by an in-progress part 2, a contrasting study in a problem setting where there exists no 1-pass shortcut. It additionally motivates further exploration into the development of monitoring tools for understanding both the intra- and inter-token computation in looped transformers.

(A note from me: compute limited how many seeds I could run. The mechanism results for the one-layer model, the Huginn-style loop and the sandwich-norm loop, and the training fix, are at two seeds; the training ablations are at one, with a few baselines repeated at a second, and there was no hyperparameter sweep. The remaining checks are at one seed. I mark each result with its seed count.)

Disclaimer: still a draft, some sections contain draft prose written w/ Claude.

Foreword: Somewhere to Start

In the accompanying essay motivating this project in the first place, I argue that the task of monitoring the models built around reasoning with latent thoughts will take tools that read these thoughts itself, not just the model output. Any such tool has to be checked against some ground truth. In order to trust a measurement instrument, we need to know what we’re supposed to read; for a frontier model, we typically don’t. A cleaner place to start might be a problem setting where models learn an algorithm we already know.

The one-layer transformer trained on modular addition is one of the best-understood examples in mech interp: it adds by representing numbers as rotations about clocks. This project constructs a multi-hop extension of the same task as a natural testbed for comparing what a loop does with its extra depth against the ground truth of standard transformer behavior.

Background and Experiment Setup

The setup is modified from the same Progress Measures for Grokking paper mentioned earlier. The original setup trains a one-layer transformer with learned positional embeddings and no normalization to predict $(a+b) \bmod 113$, with prompts of the shape a b = . The answer is read off at the token =. The original approach trains on 30% of the $113^2$ possible input pairs, leaving the other 70% for testing. They use full-batch AdamW with $\lambda=1$. In their work they fully reverse engineer the addition algorithm being used by the model, resulting in the famous “clock” algorithm. Since this task is small and the baseline is well-known, it felt like a strong testbed for this study.

Data

Like the original setup, the model sees a chain of numbers to add and a = token. There are no operators in between, and we read off = as well. The vocab is thus the 113 numbers 0 through 112, plus =.

I used the 1-hop chain data to successfully reproduce the results from Nanda et al.. For 2 and 3 hops, I sample 15,000 training chains each, built from pairs seen in the 1-hop data. Ideally the hop counts get equal samples, but since 1-hop has a maximum of 12,769 combinations and we need a held-out set, I instead let each hop count get its own batch and average the losses with equal weight.

Validating 1-hop chains uses the unseen validation pairs, and 2-/3-hop chains get 2,000 unseen chains of training pairs each. From here on we consider a model “grokked” once its validation accuracy, averaged across 1-, 2-, and 3-hop chains, reaches 0.9. To test depth generalization I also built 4-, 5-, and 6-hop chains out of training pairs.

One caveat about the task: since addition is commutative, a chain doesn’t necessarily need to be summed left to right. It is also established in the literature that shortcuts like this exist for tasks of this kind, and that trained transformers can find them. Nothing here is forcing the looped models to iterate, and this study asks exactly what goes on in the recurrent block when a looped transformer is trained on a task like this.

Models

I compare three canonical model families in this study, namely the standard transformer, a plain looped transformer, and a variation on the Huginn setup with a dedicated set of prelude/coda layers and state injection. An overview of their differences is below.

  One-layer Plain loop Huginn-style loop
Layers 1 1, shared across passes prelude (1), shared core (1), coda (1)
Passes in training 1 8 sampled each step, 1–24 (mean 8)
Passes at evaluation 1 8 8
Initial state n/a the embedding random noise, redrawn every forward pass
Input after pass 1 n/a none prelude output re-injected every pass
Norms none state-norm: on the state after each pass; sandwich-norm: around each sublayer, plus on the state sandwich norms
Readout unembed at = unembed the final state at = coda and a final norm, then unembed
Backprop full through all 8 passes through the last 4 passes

All models share Nanda et al.’s widths ($d_\text{model} = 128$, 4 heads of size 32, $d_\text{mlp} = 512$), untied embedding and unembedding matrices, and NoPE (no positional embeddings). Norms here are RMSNorms.

Training Recipe + Instability

For direct comparison, models were initially trained with the exact recipe from Nanda et al.: I used full-batch AdamW with their learning rate of $10^{-3}$, $\lambda=1$, and $\beta = (0.9, 0.98)$, and a 10-step warmup with a fixed learning rate beyond it. This was intentional so the looped models could be compared directly with the one-layer model the recipe was intended for. I train the standard transformer for 40k steps to replicate their results, and train the rest of the models for 20k steps.

An interesting problem: for the normalized deep and looped models, this Nanda recipe proved to be quite unstable quite quickly. The loss entered a cycle of constant spiking, and the models that were able to grok anyway would lose and regain their accuracy, much like the periodic behavior Lobacheva et al. describe for training with normalization and weight decay. Unshared layers did it too, so this wasn’t a loops issue.

What worked for fixing this was a two-phase schedule built on the initial observations from the highly noisy runs. Each run in the suite takes Nanda’s recipe to 14k steps before enabling gradient clipping and learning rate decay to control oscillation. This held performance in all 5 two-phase runs that grokked across two different seeds, and ended at a validation accuracy of at least 0.99. The comparison which kept the fixed learning rate did not hold the same way. The schedule also doesn’t guarantee grokking. The state-norm loop, despite using this schedule, didn’t grok at seed 42 in 20k steps. There was additionally no compute for large hyperparameter sweeps, so all of this holds under this joint recipe only. The mechanism results below use the final checkpoints of these two-phase runs; the one-layer model stays on Nanda’s recipe.

Additional ablation results, and an appendix with the ablation figures, are coming in an update to this post.

Results and Discussion

Observation 1: Attention Averaging

A good place to start is how the models use their attention to read information from the input. In theory, a loop working through the chain left-to-right would move attention from one token to the next across passes. The figure below shows this isn’t what I observed. In all loops, attention from = is spread evenly over the entire chain. This is true in every block, pass, head, and chain length. Normalized entropy for this spread is at least 0.999 everywhere, so we’re pretty close to about as evenly as the model could possibly spread its attention. This is also not special in the = token; in 3-hop chains, every position averages over the tokens it can see through the causal mask. This figure shows the attention maps from = in each head of each model, at the first pass from the seed 41 run. The other passes and results from seed 42 look the same.

This behavior is closer to what you’d expect from the one-layer model doing this arithmetic. Since attention is the only way to move information from the inputs to the $=$ token in a one-layer model, and since addition is commutative, averaging attention is enough. Where the one-layer model differs is the = token itself: some heads actually learn to put little weight on it (around 0.01, against 0.12 for an even split at 6 hops), namely 2 of 4 heads at seed 41 and 3 of 4 at seed 42. The rest weight it as if it were a number, or even a bit more.

So the loops and the one-layer model gather their inputs the same way, with a near-uniform average of the chain: the one-pass shortcut from the setup. Nothing in the loops’ attention changes from pass to pass. The rest of the results look at what the models compute from that average, and when.

Observation 2: A Clock Readout

Once the numbers are averaged at =, the model still has to turn them into an answer. Nanda et al.’s one-layer model reads its answer off a clock: the logit for each candidate answer $c$ is a sum of $\cos(w(a+b-c))$ over a few key frequencies $w$, which peaks at the right answer. I fit the same form to every model’s logits on the 1-hop grid and ask how much of the readout it explains.

The figure measures this three ways. The left panel shows the gini coefficient of each weight matrix’s norm over the 56 frequencies (0 if it’s spread evenly, 1 if it all sits on one frequency), for the embedding $W_E$ over the input numbers and the unembedding $W_U$ over the answers. The middle panel fits $\cos$ and $\sin$ of $w(a+b-c)$ at the readout’s top $k$ frequencies to the logits and shows the share of their variance it explains. The right panel removes those same frequencies from the logits and shows the loss on the training pairs: if the clock carries the answer, the loss should climb to that of a uniform guess, $\ln 113 \approx 4.73$. The dotted lines mark chance: a random matrix’s gini on the left, a readout with no clock in the middle, and a uniform guess on the right. The gini coefficient and the loss with the key frequencies removed (the “excluded loss”) follow Nanda et al.’s progress measures.

Every run reads its answer off a clock, except one. The one-layer model’s clock uses about 5 frequencies: they explain 0.84 and 0.88 of its logits’ variance (seeds 41 and 42), and adding more frequencies adds nothing. The loops spread theirs over about 20 frequencies, which explain 0.86 to 0.94. Removing those 20 frequencies from the logits pushes the loops’ loss on the training pairs close to that of a uniform guess, so the clock carries the answer rather than just fitting it. (The one-layer model’s loss overshoots a uniform guess when its top 5 frequencies are removed, because its remaining logits are large and confidently wrong; that’s the scale of its logits, not a bigger clock.) The unembedding is also far more concentrated on a few frequencies than the embedding: a gini of 0.43–0.48 against 0.17–0.32, where a random matrix gives 0.02.

The exception is the sandwich-norm loop at seed 41. Its top 20 frequencies explain only 0.40 of its logits’ variance, removing them barely changes its loss, and its unembedding is barely concentrated at all (gini 0.09). It doesn’t extrapolate to 6 hops either. Its seed-42 twin has a clock like the others, so which solution the sandwich-norm loop finds depends on the seed. One difference between the two runs: the seed-41 run grokked late, at step 18,800, after the switch to clipping and learning rate decay, while the seed-42 run grokked at step 8,000. Whether that’s why it found a different solution is untested.

Only the readout is clearly a clock, though. The embeddings lean toward the readout’s frequencies (58–85% of the embedding’s squared norm sits on the readout’s top 20 frequencies, against 36% for an even spread), but much less sharply than the unembedding, and most MLP neurons don’t follow a single frequency. How each model computes the sum before the readout isn’t established here.

The clocks also line up with the 6-hop gap from the tl;dr. If a clock came straight from an even average of the chain, it would shrink as the chain gets longer, since averaging more numbers dilutes each one: to 0.38 of its 1-hop size at 6 hops. The one-layer model’s clock shrinks a little faster than that, to 0.28 and 0.30, and its 6-hop accuracy is 0.60 and 0.79. The loops’ clocks barely shrink, staying at 0.81–0.91 of their 1-hop size, and their 6-hop accuracy is 0.88–0.93. Why the loops’ clocks hold up isn’t tested; one guess is that their norms rescale the average. The comparison also crosses recipes: the one-layer model was trained on Nanda’s recipe for 40k steps, and the loops on the two-phase schedule for 20k.

Observation 3: Compute Early, Read Late

The loops run their shared block 8 times, so we can stop them after any pass and ask two questions: does the model’s output already give the right answer, and is the answer already in the state? For the second, I fit a linear probe from the state at =, the vector the unembedding reads, to the answer on half the chains, and score it on the other half.

In the figure, each run’s probe is in colour and its output in grey, with 1-hop chains as filled circles and 3-hop chains as hollow squares; the dotted line is chance, 1/113. All three are final checkpoints, trained at 8 passes. The starred panel is the seed-41 sandwich-norm loop, the run without a clock.

In the plain loops, the answer is in the state long before the model outputs it. After a single pass at 1 hop, the probe reads the answer with 0.92 accuracy in the state-norm loop (seed 41) and 0.93 in the sandwich-norm loop (seed 42), while the model’s own output is at chance. The output only catches up at pass 6 or 7.

More hops make the computation take longer, but not the output. From 1 to 3 hops, the first pass at which the probe reaches 0.9 moves 2–4 passes later (1 → 4, 1 → 5 and 4 → 6 in the three runs), while the output moves by at most one (6 → 6, 7 → 7 and 7 → 8). The output always arrives near the training depth of 8, whatever the chain length. So even though attention looks the same in every pass, the answer takes longer to form on longer chains; the loop doesn’t do everything in its first pass.

The seed-41 sandwich-norm loop, the one without a clock, computes late too: its probe after pass 1 reads only 0.15 at 1 hop. But its probe still leads its output.

The Huginn-style loop is left out of the figure, since its probe and output are both at 0.97–1.00 from the first pass. That isn’t because its loop is faster. Its prelude computes most of the answer before the loop starts (a probe right after the prelude reads 0.87 and 0.80 at 1 hop, at seeds 41 and 42), and its coda finishes it. As the next section shows, by the end of training it barely uses what it carries between passes.

This is a toy version of the internal monitoring the essay argues for: in the plain loops, a linear readout of the state sees the answer several passes before the model’s output does. The probe only shows that the answer is linearly decodable from the state, not that the model uses it there, but for a monitor, being able to read it early is the point.

Observation 4: How the Loops Use Their Depth

Every model here is accurate at 8 passes, the depth it’s trained and evaluated at (for the Huginn-style loop, the mean of its sampled training depths). The differences show up when the loop runs longer than it was trained for, or when what it carries from pass to pass is replaced.

The plain loops break past their training depth. Their accuracy goes from 0.99–1.00 at pass 8 to 0.00–0.01 by pass 256 (the sandwich-norm loop at two seeds, the state-norm loop at one). In the sandwich-norm loop the state is unstable: a 1% nudge to it after pass 8 grows to the size of the state itself by pass 256. The answer appears near pass 8 and doesn’t stay.

The two-phase Huginn-style loop holds: it’s still at 1.00 at pass 256 at both seeds, and a 1% nudge to its state shrinks to almost nothing (below $10^{-8}$). It holds, but it has also stopped using its state. Replacing the carried state with fresh noise at every pass leaves its accuracy at 1.00 at both seeds, and the part of its input projection that reads the state has a spectral norm of only 0.06–0.07, against 0.43–0.71 for the part that reads the injected input. Zeroing the injected input instead collapses its outputs on 2-hop chains to one or two distinct answers. So by the end of training, each pass works only from the re-injected input, and every pass computes nearly the same thing.

That wasn’t always true during training. At both seeds it still relied on its state at step 16,038, after the switch to clipping and learning rate decay (accuracy with noise as the state: 0.35 and 0.15), and it ignored the state by step 20,000. Before that, its reliance went up and down, and five checkpoints can’t place the last change more precisely than “during the decay phase”. At seed 42, the Huginn-style run that kept a constant learning rate is the same run until step 14k, and it ends training relying on its state (0.01 with noise as the state). That’s a single pair, and clipping and learning rate decay switched on together, so I can’t say which of them, if either, is responsible.

Accuracy at the training depth hides all of this. One loop’s answer exists only around pass 8, and the other’s doesn’t depend on what it carries between passes. Checking a looped model’s behavior at the depth it was trained at says little about what its loop is doing.

Discussion

On a task with a one-pass shortcut, sharing a block across passes didn’t produce a step-by-step algorithm. Every loop gathered its inputs with the same even average as the one-layer model, and every run but one read its answer off a clock like it. The extra depth still shows up, but in timing rather than in the algorithm: in the plain loops the answer is decodable early, takes longer to form on longer chains, and is read out near the training depth whatever the chain length. For monitoring, that cuts both ways. A linear probe of the state sees the answer passes before the output does, which is the kind of signal an internal monitor would look for. But accuracy at the training depth hid real differences in how the loops use their depth, and a behavioral check at that depth wouldn’t have caught them.

This is one small task, with a shortcut the models can take, and small models. Most results are at two seeds, and the state-norm loop and the constant-learning-rate comparison are at one. There was no hyperparameter sweep. The plain and Huginn-style loops differ in several ways at once (prelude and coda, input injection, the random start, sampled depth and truncated backprop), so I can’t say which of those causes which behavior, and the one-layer model was trained on a different recipe from the loops. A linear probe shows that the answer is decodable from the state, not that the model uses it. How the sum is computed before the readout, and why the loops’ clocks don’t dilute, are still open.

The natural next step is a task where the shortcut isn’t available. Composing permutations in $S_5$ is the standard example: Liu et al. show that, unless a widely believed complexity conjecture fails, a fixed-depth transformer can’t solve it for arbitrarily long chains, so the depth a model needs grows with the chain. On related tasks, weight tying has been found to favor serial solutions, and looped models have been shown to spend successive passes on successive steps of the algorithm. Part 2 runs the same pipeline and probes there, to see whether the computation moves into the loop once the shortcut is gone, and whether the state still shows the answer before the output does.

entry.summary: Brief results blog post for part 1 of a 2-part study on the nature of the computation that happens inside the looping component of a looped transformer, this time on a task that needs no iterative computation. Motivated by studying the impact of increased serial depth on monitorability. Reproduction code for data and figures is here.

entry.title: Serial Depth, Monitorability, and Interpretability in Looped Transformers (Essay)

link.title: Serial Depth, Monitorability, and Interpretability in Looped Transformers (Essay)

entry.content:
tl;dr: CoT monitoring is both a heavily relied-on and fragile tool. The case for CoT monitoring leans on an architectural assumption: models have too little per-token computation power to reason without verbalizing their thoughts. Looped transformers (those that run a core set of layers for multiple iterations) are built to relax this exact constraint. I argue this poses concern for our ability to reasonably monitor the behavior of these models in the future, draw on empirical evidence to support the argument, and address counterarguments. I conclude by arguing for monitoring tools that observe what the model cannot control, rather than what the model chose to show it.

Bad Bets

In the current landscape of AI safety, monitoring the chain of thought (CoT) is the “primary bet” for detecting and preventing agentic misalignment. The unfortunate contradiction, as Jakub Pachocki writes in his blog post “An Alien Mind”, is that “evaluations indicate our ability to rely on CoT monitoring is progressively diminishing.” Despite this, the GPT-6 family system card outlines a safety system built around a central pipeline that “reviews the agent’s chain of thought alongside its actions.”

The argument for CoT monitoring in the first place is somewhat architectural. We assume the model offloads the necessary computation to produce an answer to its reasoning tokens because it has a fixed computation budget (i.e., serial depth) per forward pass. This assumption is built on empirical observation with existing models, yet it is central to our belief that the CoT carries the true thoughts of a model in the first place.

My question is this: if an increase in serial depth means a potential violation of this assumption, how big of an impact could that have on our ability to monitor our models? As a model increases in per-token computation capacity, it is empirically observed that the CoT becomes less and less necessary for sequential computation. My concern with this direction is that this independence from the CoT could bring with it a higher risk of CoT obfuscationWherein, the CoT is altered to hide misaligned intent and/or action. in subsequent model generations. However, this concern is not new to the field.

This core CoT monitorability position paper, written by researchers from across the frontier labs and academia, identifies CoT monitoring as a fragile opportunity in its title, and warns the field about making research decisions that pressure the model to obfuscate the CoT in its abstract. In fact, OpenAI themselves have even published work on the risks of obfuscation. Despite the attention on the topic of monitorability and the importance of avoiding obfuscation, recent work has shown models are capable of obfuscating the CoT through output supervision, training on documents about monitoring, and in some cases even pure prompt pressure.

Threat Vectors and the Limits of Boundedness

My stance is that looped transformers introduce a distinct threat to CoT monitorability as they seek to directly alleviate the serial depth limitation of existing transformer architectures. At a literal level, a looped transformer just runs a core block several times per token. Thus the amount of computation we can fit into a token is governed by loop iterations, not layer count. While a standard transformer is inherently limited in depth, a looped transformer can potentially trade additional compute for extra serial depth. The idea is that this tradeoff could enable additional reasoning within each token and increase the potential for CoT obfuscation and other undesirable outcomes.

To be more precise about where computation happens, I borrow a taxonomy from user Skye on LessWrong, who was in the lab responsible for Ouro. They break down monitorability concerns into those relating to intra-token computation (or “computation within a single timestep (before the model commits to a token)”), and those relating to inter-token computation (or “computation from one timestep to the next”).

Skye makes a natural objection to my point, being that a model’s serial depth is bounded, however much looping increases it. The core of their argument is that inter-token computation poses the bigger danger in the long term, since the masked inter-token computation is the most direct pathway to obfuscating the CoT. While I mostly agree with this point, I’m a bit hesitant to accept the implication that scaling the serial depth ceiling without further safeguards in place is inherently a non-issue purely because depth remains finite.

The issue is that bounded or not, the extra depth looping buys relaxes the exact same serial depth constraint that CoT monitoring leans onQuick aside: there's some intuition to be gained for the benefit of increased depth by breaking down classic results from deep learning theory. The universal approximation theorem tells us that a wide enough ReLU net with one hidden layer can produce an $\epsilon$-close approximation of any continuous function on a bounded domain, out of piecewise linear components. A classic follow-up result is the manner in which the amount of expressible piecewise linear components grows with width and depth. While expressivity grows polynomially in width, it grows exponentially in depth. That exponential is a ceiling on what a network can express, though, not necessarily what emerges in practice. Empirically, networks tend to realize far fewer piecewise linear components, with a less than exponential gain from depth. Still, depth was always an intriguing scaling axis; the concern is that looping could add arbitrary depth without extra parameters.. Recent exploration suggests that relaxing the serial depth constraint can translate to a real capability increase. The cited work shows that increasing serial depth even logarithmically with the input length lets a transformer solve reasoning tasks that complexity theory states fixed-depth transformers cannot, and that scaling depth is actually more efficient than scaling the number of CoT steps. To hammer this point home: Saunshi et al. show that a looped transformer has the ability to effectively simulate $T$ steps of CoT reasoning output with $T$ loops, generating “latent thoughts” that never appear as output tokens themselves.

Put simply, a monitor fails when a model has both the no-CoT ability to carry a hidden line of reasoning and enough control over its CoT to obfuscate it. In Skye’s terms, the first is a question of intra-token computation, the work done before each token is committed, while the second governs what the inter-token channel, the CoT itself, actually shows. Neel Nanda notes that these appear to be separate abilities: “controllability seems very dependent on details of post-training, while no CoT reasoning is largely determined by the pretrain.” Since looping is an architectural and thus a pretraining decision, it has the potential to move the no-CoT axis directly, independent of post-training. So I think the potential for CoT obfuscation along both axes, no-CoT ability and controllability, should be studied.

Star Signs and Mind Reading

So we know there is some evidence in the literature supporting the idea that loops could bring about increased hidden reasoning capability. But how relevant is looping today? Well, the last year and a half or so has seen the publication of a substantial number of open LoopLMsTerm describing language models built around looped transformers, from the Ouro paper. including Huginn, the aforementioned Ouro, Nanbeige, and ParcaeFor some more evidence that looping is viewed as an additional axis for scaling, the Parcae paper even includes its own scaling laws for looping.. Beyond the open releases, there has been discussion of looped transformers making their way into frontier labs. Much of this concern has focused on GPT-6 Astra in particular. According to Neel Nanda, Astra can do a “concerning amount” with no CoT.

Earlier I cited LatentMathBench, a benchmark which disables the CoT and asks a model to work through a sequence of arithmetic assignments, measuring how many steps it can handle while still answering correctly half the time. On this measure, Astra’s horizon is roughly 4× that of the next best OpenAI model, GPT-5.6 Sol, and 7× that of GPT-4. The size of this jump is hard to ignore.

Beyond the serial depth jump, the CoT traces that models like Astra do produce are becoming increasingly controllable. Work done as recently as March of this year found there existed little to no controllability over CoT in frontier language models, using the same evaluation suite (CoT-Control) that OpenAI reported in their official Astra safety overview in early September. According to that September overview, Astra has a 60.9% controllability rate. This is a massive jump from the also-reported 16.1% for GPT-5.6 Sol and 1.7% for GPT-5.5 Thinking.These rates are for CoT traces between 750 and 1,250 tokens long. Possibly the most damning detail is that some of this behavior shows up unprompted: the same safety overview reports that “under simple monitoring-awareness (without being told to evade the monitor), [Astra] spontaneously generates substantially fewer chain-of-thought tokens.” In adversarial evaluations, the overview adds, it “can sometimes evade our internal monitors when asked to perform certain sabotage tasks.”

To be fair, OpenAI has stated that it attributes Astra’s increased CoT controllability to a capability increase rather than an architectural difference. Astra’s looped design is still only reported rather than confirmed, and some read the decline in CoT trace length generated as a stronger model writing shorter traces. But a stronger model needing less CoT is exactly the concern: the shorter the trace, the less of the model’s reasoning it carries. My argument, however, does not depend on the increase coming from architectural changes. I simply view architectural changes as the easiest path to a significant jump in serial depth. The reason that I focus on architecture in particular over plain capability is the figure presented above. Astra sits well off the trend line the other models share.

Perhaps the most interesting counterargument I came across was from the commenters on R. Arike’s LessWrong post on a similar topic, focused on Astra. The comments section includes some valuable discussion, including the argument that since a loop’s intermediate states could be decodable, looping might actually help with monitoring, and others even reported decoding them in open LoopLMs like Huginn and Ouro. As Arike notes in a reply, though, this is “pretty similar to using the logit lens,” and “substantially worse than proper CoT, but better than nothing.” I think this is a direction worth studying more deeply, but not one I’d take as reassurance, and certainly not an end-all-be-all solution. As it stands, we don’t have many strongly reliable tools for this kind of latent mind reading, at the token level or the CoT level. However, this doesn’t have to be the case!

Taking a Deeper Look

My claim is this: when the distribution of emitted tokens is highly controllable and enough serial computation fits within a single forward pass, a monitor built around reading from those emitted tokens is reading what the model chose to show it. Reliable monitoring tools for the next generation of latent reasoners must touch the computation itself.

So… what does that look like?

At the moment, I’m honestly unsure if there’s a single answer out there. Worthwhile tools for this job could take any number of shapes.

Some could even act before the model exists at all, like in the data. Data-first approaches to this are already out there, and show potential for more robust alignment of downstream models. These are grounded in the idea that model unlearning is too powerful to rely purely on post-training interventions, and pre-training interventions seem more robust.

Another potential direction is algorithmic improvement at the pre-training stage. The motivation for this comes from the same Neel Nanda post describing the separation between CoT controllability and No-CoT reasoning ability. If we care about ensuring the model is behaving as intended without reliance on the CoT, then maybe it makes sense to ensure the stages of training most impactful on No-CoT computation are well-aligned, as well. As it currently stands, we don’t have many methods for doing so at a method level.

Others could attempt to monitor the computation itself, akin to the “mind reader” imagery from earlier. I think of this idea (in the best of all possible worlds) as upgrading from user space to kernel access: a model might struggle to keep things hidden the deeper and deeper we dig. However, this approach and others like it tell a story as old as the field itself: algorithmic pressure on the interpretability signals is a dangerous game.

Whatever shape the winning tool might take in the coming years, the goal is the same: monitorability. Mechanistic interpretability itself should be viewed as a means here, not the end. What really matters is whether the tool we choose still tells us something true about what the model is doing, even when the model would rather it didn’t. We should be satisfied by reliability of any mechanistic or otherwise internal tools to at least the same degree as we are by the CoT.

To this end, tools for disentangling latent thoughts face the same optimization pressure concerns that currently threaten the CoT. Bailey et al. show that the model activations themselves can be modified through the prompt itself or through fine-tuning to evade internal probes and monitoring tools, all the while allowing the undesirable behavior to continue. The lesson we’re seemingly learning from CoT monitoring carries over: if we choose to read from some oracle inside the model, we should think twice about putting any optimization pressure on it.

Until now, the CoT has been a reliable tool because models think out loud by necessity. Increasing serial computation depth is one of the most direct ways that necessity could be broken. If it is, the monitors worth building are those that read what the model cannot control, rather than what it chose to show them. Whether such a lens exists that can withstand optimization pressure is perhaps a bigger question.

entry.title: IntAct (Interpretable Activations for Reward Hacking)
entry.content:
One thing I noticed pretty quickly when exploring mech interp through the lens of reward hacking was how much control I wanted to have over sampling, collecting, and processing large batches of activations. A second thing I noticed was the lack of canonical testbeds for studying particular phenomena in the field. The result of this was aopatric/intact.

what intact is

intact is built around a single canonical setup which consistently produces distinguishable reward hacking behavior in Qwen3-4B. The setup and environment are borrowed (and credited) from ariahw/rl-rewardhacking, as are their graders and classification rules for hacks/non-hacks.

The goal of intact is to enable the user to rapidly collect activations from reward-hacking rollouts of Qwen3-4B with high prompt granularity, and quickly load those activations into experimental scripts with the library’s exposed Python API. The library achieves this by maintaining a few desired invariants:

  • reproducibility: all rollouts are stored with exact token IDs sampled from vLLM at explicit, recorded settings; labels are provided by upstream’s own grader and are consistent across every prompt variant; alignment checks in the API’s backend ensure consistent loading and ensure that the offline stored activations match what the online hook sees up to 4e-5 relative error
  • ease of use: function names are borrowed from existing common APIs to easily transition (pandas, numpy, Hugging Face datasets, TransformerLens); generations store an anchor corresponding to beginning of the definition of the overwritten reward function, and querying for activations is possible relative to the anchor itself

what it isn’t

intact doesn’t seek to replace existing libraries for activation collection in interpretability like TransformerLens or nnsight. Both of these libraries are extremely useful in their own right and provide more generalist tooling for working on interpretability through the lens of activations, but neither targets the same questions as intact and that’s okay.

Whereas nnsight wraps a model and allows for runtime interventions, intact does its activation capture offline and simply provides an interface through which to manage the growing collection of tensors on disk.

TransformerLens in particular re-implements model architectures with hooks for analysis, so we can perform forward passes and return a given set of activations we query by name. It’s also a library built for intervention and exists as the standard for mech interp on its supported architectures for a reason. Notably, however, its standard weight processing changes the weights that you would typically see relative to an equivalent Hugging Face model.

intact seeks to do neither of these things. Instead, it’s a tool built for batch runs sampling rollouts and activations to ask many different questions about one, unique, controlled thing. Existing tooling lets us ask a more limited amount of questions about a more broad class of things.

why so particular?

The motivation behind narrowing in on a single canonical example was a combination of a frustration with the lack of widely employed reward hacking toy problems and that with the lack of tooling for identifying patterns in large quantities of activations.

intact hopes to serve that niche; those who are asking fewer questions about a broad set of behaviors, and more particular questions about this one isolated behavioral example.

plans, updates, notes

note: many of the experiments i had originally planned to use this base for have been put on hold for now; updates will come to aid QoL and fix known issues with the library, but for now the included probe_smoke.py takes in activations and spits out results for probe success at a specified layer with specified parameters.

status: v0.1 covers the rh-s1 adapter end to end. On upstream’s evaluation prompts, rh-s1 reward-hacks in 73.7% of 1,130 rollouts (113 test problems × 10), with 18.7% “Correct; Attempted Reward Hack”, against the ~79% and ~14% upstream reports, pooled over several seeds. Sampling isn’t reproducible from seeds on upstream’s vLLM version, so rollouts are stored rather than regenerated.

install

intact needs a CUDA GPU for sampling and activation extraction, and Python 3.12. Reading saved data needs neither. Install from git:

uv add "intact-interp @ git+https://github.com/aopatric/intact@v0.1"

Sampling and grading also need a clone of upstream’s repo at a pinned commit. intact doesn’t redistribute it, since upstream has no license. The setup steps are in the README.

thanks for reading!

entry.title: Finding the Edge of Stability for LLM Post-Training

link.title: Finding the Edge of Stability for LLM Post-Training

entry.content:
tl;dr: does the training behavior of language models in post-training share a generally accepted characteristic observed in full-batch training at small scale? previous attempt said no, but a revisit showed that was a weak claim. re-attempt ended inconclusively, but included rounds of iteration that taught me more about research engineering than a successful one would have.

(note: since this revisit was meant as an exploration and less of a publication, there were no novel figures generated beyond those in tensorboard. figures in this writeup come from existing literature and are cited as such.)

The Edge of Stability?

Much of modern deep learning’s success is attributed to gradient descent (GD). In recent years, a wave of research effort has been dedicated toward understanding the geometry of learning in neural nets trained with GD. The Edge of Stability (EoS) is one product of that effort: it describes a deviation, observed in practice, from standard results in optimization theory about gradient descent on twice-differentiable losses. The argument generally goes as follows:

We can take any sufficiently smooth ($\in C^2$) loss function $f( heta)$ and consider a second-order Taylor approximation within some neighborhood of a local minimum $ heta^{\ast}$, where $H = abla^2 f( heta^\ast)$ is the Hessian at the minimum:

\[ egin{align*} f( heta) & = f( heta^{\ast}) + abla f( heta^{\ast})^ op ( heta - heta^{\ast}) + rac 1 2 ( heta - heta^{\ast})^ op H ( heta - heta^{\ast}) + o(\| heta - heta^\ast\|^2) \ & \approx f( heta^\ast) + abla f( heta^\ast)^ op ( heta - heta^\ast) + rac 1 2 ( heta - heta^\ast)^ op H ( heta - heta^\ast) \end{align*}\]

Since $ heta^{\ast}$ is a stationary point, $ abla f( heta^{\ast}) = 0$. Taking the gradient of this approximation gives:

\[ abla f( heta) \approx abla f( heta^{\ast}) + H( heta - heta^{\ast}) = H( heta - heta^{\ast})\]

So consider the gradient update step:

\[ egin{align*} heta_{t+1} & = heta_t - \eta abla f( heta_t) \ & \approx heta_t - \eta H ( heta_t - heta^{\ast}) \end{align*}\]

Under this approximation, subtracting $ heta^{\ast}$ from both sides lets us express this relationship in terms of the update performed by gradient descent on the error vector to the optimum, $\delta_t = heta_t - heta^\ast$, for each time step:

\[ egin{align*} heta_{t+1} - heta^{\ast} & = ( heta_t - heta^{\ast}) - \eta H ( heta_t - heta^{\ast}) \ \delta_{t+1} & = (I - \eta H) \delta_t. \end{align*}\]

This reveals that under this second-order approximation, each gradient update multiplies $\delta_t$ by $(I - \eta H)$, and along any eigendirection $ u_i$ of $H$ the error is scaled by $(1 - \eta \lambda_i)$. So we can treat this gradient descent update like any other linear mapping, and consider the top eigendirection $ u^\ast$ of $H$, with eigenvalue $\lambda_ ext{max}$. Since we took $ heta^\ast$ to be a local minimum, the second-order necessary condition for smooth objectives forces $H \succeq 0$. A positive semi-definite (PSD) $H$ forces all of its eigenvalues $\lambda_i \geq 0$, so $\lambda_ ext{max}$ is also the largest eigenvalue in magnitude, and $ u^\ast$ is the first eigendirection along which training becomes unstable as $\eta$ grows. For $\delta_t$ to converge to $0$ along $ u^\ast$ as $t o \infty$, we need $\lvert 1 - \eta \lambda_ ext{max} vert < 1$. But:

\[ egin{align*} | 1 - \eta \lambda_ ext{max} | < 1 & \iff 1 - \eta \lambda_ ext{max} < 1 \quad ext{and} \quad -1 + \eta \lambda_ ext{max} < 1 \ & \iff 0 < \lambda_ ext{max} \quad ext{and} \quad \lambda_ ext{max} < rac 2 \eta. \end{align*}\]

The first condition holds automatically for any nonzero PSD Hessian. The second condition is key; it tells us that when we are near a local minimum, curvature $\lambda_ ext{max} > rac 2 \eta$ creates local instability, causing the error vector to oscillate with growing magnitude along $ u^\ast$ with each training step (at exactly $\lambda_ ext{max} = rac 2 \eta$, it oscillates without shrinking). A similar argument applies to a quadratic model around any iterate of gradient descent, not just a minimum, which led to the longstanding belief that gradient descent on neural networks is unstable in regions where the sharpness ($\lambda_ ext{max}$) exceeds $ rac 2 \eta$.

Despite this analytic result, the original Cohen et al. (2021) paper observed a two-stage phenomenon in practice when training neural networks with full-batch GD: a phase of progressive sharpening (wherein the local $\lambda_ ext{max}$ at iteration $t$ starts low and rises steadily to the $ rac 2 \eta$ threshold) and a phase of stable oscillation (wherein the local curvature hovers around the $ rac 2 \eta$ threshold while the loss continues to decrease, albeit non-monotonically). These observations contradicted the predictions made by the second-order approximation and at the time raised several questions as to the nature of this phenomenon, including whether EoS is intrinsic to gradient descent on neural networks in practice. Since then, much work has expanded upon the original EoS paper, including many asking similar questions about learning geometry in new learning contexts.

In particular, the EoS umbrella has grown to include analogous phenomena for stochastic gradient descent (Andreyev & Beneventano 2024) and for adaptive optimizers (Cohen et al. 2022). Recent work has even used EoS as a tool for building new analytic frameworks for neural network optimization, including proving generalization bounds by modeling SGD as a random dynamical system that converges to a fractal attractor at the EoS (Tuci et al. 2026). Nevertheless, the extent to which EoS emerges in language model post-training, if at all, remains largely unexplored.

Aside: Why Post-Training?

To be fair, I first came across both EoS and this question in a list of curated term project topics for MIT’s 6.7910 Statistical Learning Theory, and later took it on as my term project for 6.7960 Deep Learning. However, I chose to investigate it because post-training differs from most of the settings studied in the EoS literature: it shifts the domain, the target, and, in practice, the learning rate, all of which can affect how much EoS shapes the learning trajectory. The learning rate is the most interesting of the three. Fine-tuning typically uses learning rates one to two orders of magnitude smaller than pretraining, so for plain GD the stability threshold $ rac 2 \eta$ is huge: at $\eta = 10^{-5}$, it sits at $200{,}000$. Does the sharpness of a pretrained model ever climb to meet a threshold that high within a fine-tuning run, or does post-training simply never reach the edge? That question isn’t obvious a priori, and it’s the one this project set out to answer. For simplicity, I chose to structure my approach around the canonical first post-training stage: supervised instruction tuning.

Round one: 6.7960, Fall 2025

I originally scoped the project to include trials taking models from the Pythia suite (70M–1.4B) and fine-tuning them in an instruction-following context using the Alpaca dataset. One misstep in the original scoping was my approach to optimization. To get closer to ‘real’ instruction-tuning setups, my experiments were built around ‘realistic’ learning rates on AdamW. Additionally, since memory was a concern, there needed to be some approach to efficiently approximating $\lambda_ ext{max}$. The original project did this using a single-batch estimate of local $\lambda_ ext{max}$ with PyHessian, a probe that proved to be extremely noisy. After results seemed to show a general trend of rising overall sharpness but far too much variation to confirm EoS, the original conclusion was that EoS did not persist in post-training. At the time this decision was made after a few engineering oversights and mistakes stacked up on one another and left no clear signal that something was wrong in the experiment code.

Coming back to it

Sometime in late August, I was cleaning up some projects on my GitHub when I decided to go back and take a closer look at my original EoS project. I decided to do a full-on audit of the experiment code given I finally had the time to discern where in the chain my tooling was failing. What I discovered were the shortcomings described above, and in particular, the realization that the codebase, as presented, could not make the claim that EoS did not persist.

Further analysis let me break down the list of small issues into a few major categories:

  • invariant violations, which came down to configuration details like gradient clipping and optimizer choice.
  • estimator noise, which came down to overly trusting what was a fragile tool at best.
  • unfounded claims, which arose from a combination of the above and time constraints limiting my ability to thoroughly validate findings in time.

At that point, one major milestone to a successful revisit was clear. I needed a tool.

Rebuilding the instrument

The main focal point behind the redesign was verification before trust, i.e., no measurement was taken as valid until the tool was validated against a simple known case. This initially meant writing extra unit tests, but led to much more:

Reliable measurements of local landscape curvature: To get a strong estimate for $\lambda_ ext{max}$, the new repository includes verified custom implementations of both simple power iteration and the Lanczos algorithm, implemented in PyTorch to run efficiently on the GPU while maintaining bit-determinism. These were tested against small verified Hessians and experiments enforced agreement within $1\%$ between the two solvers to accept a measurement.

More Precision: After the swap to the new solvers, a problem began to emerge where the solvers were disagreeing and Lanczos had trouble converging. Analysis of logs revealed that due to the small learning rates, fp32 was losing $\sim 3\%$ of each update to rounding error, contributing to both drift in the solvers and divergence in the measurements. After a simple swap to fp64 at the cost of about 0.5GB of video memory, this problem resolved itself.

Careful and intentional experimentation: One shortcoming of my original approach to the project was the lack of sufficient unit tests for components. For the rebuild, each milestone in the process was assigned its own pass/fail criteria that determined whether we had successfully reached it. These included a positive-control test on a toy-scale MLP and batch GD to assert the tooling could even detect EoS in the first place.

The combination of these improvements (as well as many QoL improvements like modular sweepable configurations with Hydra and deterministic resume of paused runs) led to a repository that could be trusted to measure EoS in the post-training context.

Takeaways from the revisit

The two most significant experiments from the revisit were my positive control test and the subsequent Pythia-70m run that followed it.

For the positive control experiment, I took a small MLP and trained it on Alpaca with plain batch GD using gradient accumulation while measuring local curvature with my tooling. However, this experiment produced an interesting and unexpected result: $\lambda_ ext{max}$ on the fixed probe (size $n=64$) sat around 1.7–2.3× above the $ rac 2 \eta$ limit, while gradient descent clearly oscillated around some boundary. This motivated a revisit of the literature that led me to (Lee & Lee 2026), which argues that $\lambda_ ext{max}$ itself is a poor stability indicator in practice and finds that curvature along the step direction tends to oscillate near that $ rac 2 \eta$ threshold.

After extending the measurement infrastructure one more time to measure curvature along the step direction, the EoS picture was clear. After rerunning the trial with a step sharpness measurement, I observed step sharpness oscillating near $ rac 2 \eta$ for the final third of training after a phase of progressive sharpening. EoS!

With the tool verified as capable of detecting EoS, the next run was a test on Pythia-70m with a somewhat more realistic $\eta=7.5 \cdot 10^{-6}$ learning rate and the same batch gradient descent setup. This experiment showed promise! For this training run, the tool detected oscillation beginning around step 1100/4000, with oscillation settling at around $0.92 imes$ the $ rac 2 \eta$ limit and just barely failing the predefined test suite checking for EoS. This result is not another negative result, but rather a close null. If anything, the result warrants more investigation! The code and instructions to reproduce these runs are in the post-training-EoS repo.

Why I stopped, and what I learned

The main issue was scale. Even a cleaner lock on EoS for a 70M model on a 64-sample probe with plain gradient descent wouldn’t tell us much about how real-sized language models behave under real adaptive optimizers and learning rate schedules, and getting to the point where I can run an experiment that assesses those contexts involves compute that I simply don’t have access to at the moment.

Nonetheless, I learned a ton from this revisit. The biggest takeaway for me was that a null result is only as good as the ability to detect a positive one. Despite ending up in a similar inconclusive place as the original project, the fact that I was able to confirm EoS in a controlled environment using my custom tooling first made the rest of the process significantly more robust and streamlined.

In a context where I had the time and resources available to do more experiments, I’d run additional tests on my 70M demo and scale up to 1.4B before doing larger and larger tests to analyze the impact of model scale on the emergence of EoS, if any.

Despite the null result, this project enabled me to grow significantly as an engineer and as a researcher, and the lessons learned from the process have informed subsequent projects including my recent deep dive into mechanistic interpretability as I prepare to return to school for my MEng in the spring!

References

  • Cohen et al. Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability. ICLR 2021. arXiv:2103.00065
  • Cohen et al. Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability. 2022. arXiv:2207.14484
  • Andreyev, Beneventano. Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD. 2024. arXiv:2412.20553
  • Tuci, Korkmaz, Şimşekli, Birdal. Generalization at the Edge of Stability. 2026. arXiv:2604.19740
  • Lee, Lee. The Road Taken: The Role of Optimizers at the Edge of Stability. 2026. arXiv:2608.18415
  • Biderman et al. Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models Across Training and Scaling. ICML 2023. arXiv:2304.01373
  • Taori et al. Stanford Alpaca: An Instruction-following LLaMA Model. 2023. GitHub
  • Yao, Gholami, Keutzer, Mahoney. PyHessian: Neural Networks Through the Lens of the Hessian. IEEE BigData 2020. arXiv:1912.07145
entry.summary: Revisit of my 6.7960 term project investigating the EoS phenomenon in language model post-training. Null result, but learned a ton.
